title: Film as escapism and film as an art form.

commenti.body:
I personally don't pursue art as escapism anymore (it takes a lot of self medication for me to give up on analytical engagement). The act of reading, watching, or playing media without being able to take something informative away from it just feels like I'm being exploited. And that's intimately tied to the intent behind the media. If an author wants to impart insight--be it with respect to science, history, society, or the craft itself--it will show. If the author just wants to steal a million pennies from myopic consumers, they have little incentive to make products well, and that will show, too.

To some extent I understand *why* bread and circuses exist, but it still baffles me that so many consumers simply don't want more. I get that many aren't educated enough to even begin to appreciate the technical or literary aspects of a film. But there's still this banal element that is wholly foreign to me, that *all* they want is that singular, simple emotional blast. Villain HQ exploded, bickering couple kisses, down-to-earth person dies. The film could be totally formulaic, barebones vicarious rebellion/reclamation plot, paperthin all white male characters with token feminist-but-not-really busty chick, and deus ex magic explained by scifi bullshit jargon; but apparently the feels generated by two seconds of CGI are enough to justify admission, and maybe even the viewer's very existence. I don't want to be friends with people who live their lives waiting for the next cheap, brief visual high; it's frankly just as depressing as being friends with actual drug junkies.

And yeah, arthouse fanatics can be just as addicted to vicarious wish fulfillment. But on average, they at least find ways to contribute to the community's knowledge base and creativity, instead of just wanking off to templated, prepackaged, mass-produced fluff.

The negativity usually attributed to the escapism typical of entertainment is just a bad lesson derived from the works of critical theorists - no need to go into details here though, but I invite you to think about it again; forgetting about reality through popular movies can have, for example, strongly stabilizing effects on society as a whole, but there are instantiations which apply to individual cases, too, obviously :) Anyway, I guess one could defend a mind-independent view of aesthetic value as it was the degree of *originality* the work exhibits. Obviously there may be minor disagreements, but the great use of deep focus in Renoir's *La règle du jeu* would be a quasi-objective feature of the film in this kind of analysis. It may seem difficult to put this into practice but actually we do it partly, already (that is, we already treat innovation as a relevant property of beautiful works of art). Anyway, if you assume this view, you wouldn't have many problems accepting that we watch movies as artistic products essentially through a problem-solving approach. Basically what you do is trying to spot the constitutive elements of film *x* that exploit the potentialities of the medium in original, ground-breaking ways. This can hardly be reconnected to the escapistic conception of movies (as entertainment products). So one could have a strong theory about film interpretations that would allow her to draw a sharp line between art and entertainment when it comes to films.

> **When I feel sad or depressed I get the need to consume art, often meaningful** and not superficial like blockbusters. 

This is their point: What you just described is escapism. You have proven, albeit ironically, that there is no distinction.
I was responding to myself, This comment was from before the conversation started and I wanted to make it clear that I wasn't rejecting the existence of escapism.

There are a lot of lines you could draw between the two. I don't think it's controversial to say that there ARE those two categories, and maybe even more. In lit, you have the idea of literature vs. genre fiction. This is pretty common terminology. There, the line is drawn sort of on cliches. A work of genre fiction is built off of a bunch of cliches that respect the genre, whereas literature avoids cliches totally. You could also draw the line on style. Literature is about style in prose, whereas genre fiction usually has straightforward prose. Like I said, there are a lot of different lines.

The best single answer I have, although it's totally uninformed and I haven't read any literature on the subject, is that the art form is centrally concerned with ideas, whereas the escapism form might touch on ideas here and there, but they aren't central to the work (or, maybe, the work isn't centered on understanding/explain the ideas). If this isn't clear, then just think about your favorite film and try to find what little nugget of an idea it's trying to explore or explain. 

Anyway, this sort of discussion always gets really muddled. Partly because really, both pure escapism and art can both be entertaining and engaging, but somehow "escapism" implies that it is more entertaining than high art, which is just an unfair connotation.
You're responding to the wrong person
Then your question has nothing to do with movies, it has to do with teleology and living a purposeful life. Like, you can't actually answer your question unless you know what a Good Life actually is.

I never made any association between positive and negative with meaningfulness. I think escapism can negatively impact your life by causing you to ignore the issues in front of you in real life. It is very possible to have very meaningful, escapist experiences with art, but that doesn't mean it is positive. If you become a shut-in and just watch movies all day you can thoroughly enjoy them and experience it all as they were intended, but still be avoiding the rest of life. 

My question hinges less on what "valid" art is and how to meaningfully consume it, but where is the line between just living your life with movies as a compliment and watching movies as an escape from life.
Alright, then I didn't understand it correctly. You are right.

Sure, but the fact that you've made a value judgement between "meaningful and not superficial" means that the dichotomy between escapism and aesthetic experience the OP made is invalid in your case. I'm not saying there is no such thing as escapism, when I am sad I watch something funny, or sad, or that I feel will compliment or improve my emotional state, but the distinction between positive(meaningful) and negative(meaningless) the OP makes means escapism is a negative and meaningless act compared to meaningful consumption of more 'valid' art.

Well, I do. When I feel sad or depressed I get the need to consume art, often meaningful and not superficial like blockbusters. I watch films on a regular basis, but sometimes I have the explicit intention to watch a film just to avoid an emotional state I don't feel comfortable in, and it's kind of a therapy, because it works.

Like, this whole 'positive' 'negative' dichotomy you've invented does not seem like a useful one. You're just creating two categories where either none exist or a multiplicity of categories exist which can never fall into your dichotomy. (Specifically, while it may be tempting to categorize stuff along 'good-bad' 'positive-negative' lines, when it comes to stuff like art those distinctions are almost always knee jerk reactions. Like, it is just as easy to say "escapism is negative and artistic engagement is positive" as it is to say "Silent movies are good and talkies are bad", I think a close examination of the whole act of 'doing' or 'watching' art reveals that both aspects are at play constantly. I can read Harry Potter or the Philosophical Investigations and I will be engaging in escapism both times.)

There is no distinction, any aesthetic experience is-in some way- escapist. Why are you so fixated on intention? I've never sat down and said "boy I need to escape from life real quick let me watch this." or "boy I need to see some art right now and feel smart, I don't need to escape at all."
